## Ergogenic Effects and Exercise Modalities
Aerobic endurance is the modality with the most consistent moderate-to-large benefits, although the magnitude differs between individuals [1]. Caffeine does not directly improve maximal oxygen capacity but permits training at greater power output and longer duration, with effects demonstrated in activities lasting from 60 seconds to 2 hours [2]. For strength, recent work suggests no effect on maximal ability but enhanced resistance to fatigue [2]. 
The ISSN position stand reports that caffeine consistently improves exercise performance at doses of 3–6 mg/kg body mass, with minimal effective doses possibly as low as 2 mg/kg, while very high doses such as 9 mg/kg increase side-effect incidence without additional ergogenic benefit [1]. Low doses below 3 mg/kg (approximately 200 mg) are also ergogenic, but appear to act through central nervous system effects on vigilance, alertness, and mood rather than through alterations in peripheral whole-body exercise responses [3]. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of endurance running included 21 randomized controlled trials with caffeine doses ranging from 3 to 9 mg/kg [4]. 
The classical theory that caffeine enhances fat oxidation and spares muscle glycogen has very little support and is an incomplete explanation [2]. Peripheral mechanisms involving substrate utilization, fatigue delay, and antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions have been proposed, but non-central-nervous-system mechanisms remain largely unknown or controversial [5]. Inter-individual differences in performance response and adverse effects such as sleep disturbance or anxiety may be attributed to genetic variation in caffeine metabolism, habitual intake, and physical and psychological factors [1].
